I'm running BB10. It's most likely the best in my eyes.

The hub aggregates all communications into one stream that can be divided based on read/unread, or platform. It lets you search the entire thing too which is glorious to find older conversations or attachments. I'm able to remove the battery/add external media, unzip files, and read most file formats. It also has an android runtime environment so I can run android apps if I need/want which deals with the lack of native apps.

Also if you check out the Passport its got an amazing capacitive keyboard/display concept. The Blackberry is the only phone in roughly 7 years that I've been willing to keep for more than a year. I've had a Z10 for about 2-3 years now and I still think it's better than my housemates iPhone 6.

All the conversation aside about adoption rates of app, user interfaces becoming homogenized, etc, my answer is simple: it depends on the target audience.

I know, that doesn't really sound like a simple answer but I think it is. No one really knew how much we'd all want to browse the internet on our phones until it was presented to us. The only audience I can really see a market for at this time is privacy advocates and the only one I can see that happening with is Ubuntu. I would drop my phone in a heartbeat if Ubuntu came out with a phone that was completely open sourced code, stressed privacy from the get-go (especially encryption), and was kept up-to-date on the security side even for older phones.

I wouldn't care if it looked a little clunky, didn't have many games, and wasn't all that fast. If I can securely browse the web (securely being relative, I know), check my email, send text messages (though not necessarily though the carrier, i.e. Telegram), and make phone calls, it would be enough for me. I don't think I'm alone in this regard. It wouldn't be huge, it wouldn't take any sizable portion out of either Apple or Google's share, but it might be enough to sustain the small user base that wants that.
